#5463. NiCE’s next-generation Cognigy bets the hard part of AI agents is running them, not building them

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

The contact center has been the low-hanging fruit for the artificial intelligence industry. Ask any information technology or business leader what they want to use agentic AI for, and they will say it’s to improve the customer experience, which starts with the contact center.

However, to date, the industry has spent the past two years arguing over which AI agent is the smartest. That’s the wrong debate. Model capabilities are improving so quickly and are getting so much cheaper that raw intelligence and reasoning are becoming the least differentiated part of the stack.

The real challenge for enterprises is operating a fleet of AI agents reliably across complete customer journeys, with the visibility and control a large business requires. Without that, the human, or worse, the customer, is left connecting the dots among the outputs of the growing number of agents they are communicating with.

That’s the thesis behind the next generation of NiCE Cognigy, which NiCE Ltd. launched this week. The release includes a redesigned Agentic Experience Studio, an AI Assist companion spanning the building, testing and improvement of agents, reusable “skills” that package instructions and tools, turn-by-turn tracing and native voice-to-voice model support.

Default speech-to-text, text-to-speech and large language models are now included in the per-conversation price, with premium models from Deepgram, ElevenLabs and Anthropic available with a few clicks and billed by usage.

Ahead of the launch, I attended an analyst briefing with Nhu Ho, senior product marketing manager at NiCE Cognigy, and with Clement Boutier, director of product management, who leads the team that built the release and owns the platform roadmap.

Here are the important points from this release:

Ho opened with a chart showing how long AI can work on its own before a human has to step in. In 2020, it was seconds; in 2024, it was minutes; and this year it’s roughly 16 hours. The footnote was interesting, as it calculated that figure at a 50% success rate. “Capable and dependable do not always mean the same thing,” Ho said. “That is exactly where the platform matters.”

For CX leaders, that’s a solid benchmark to consider. A 50% success rate is a research milestone. In a contact center, it’s a churn event or a compliance violation. As models commoditize, value shifts to the system around them: testing, tracing, guardrails and deterministic fallbacks. NiCE doesn’t build frontier models, and frontier model builders don’t run contact centers. Positioning Cognigy as the layer that makes AI dependable is a smart place to plant a flag.

Cognigy earned its pre-acquisition leadership position by handling complex production deployments for large brands such as Lufthansa, Mercedes and DHL. But that flexibility and customizability added complexity. Boutier put it this way: “The large number of options when configuring an agent creates friction to get started, which slows things down.” The new studio lets a builder stand up an agent in a few clicks, with models already provisioned, while power-user tools, including full access to the agent’s system prompt, are available in advanced sections.

This is important because NiCE aims to create a “1+1=3” value proposition for its current customers. NiCE needs Cognigy to expand broadly across the CXone installed base, not just among expert teams at the largest enterprises. Boutier described three builder personas: smaller businesses building simple agents, contact center administrators and team leads, and engineers at technically sophisticated companies. AI Assist is aimed squarely at the first two.

In the demo, it built an agent, tested it, fixed the problems it found, and deployed it to WhatsApp. The flip side is that lowering the barrier means more agents built by less experienced people, which makes the governance features the real story of this release.

Despite all the agentic hype, most enterprises aren’t ready to hand over entire journeys to an autonomous agent. Boutier outlined three modes: traditional natural language understanding, hybrid and fully agentic. Hybrid “is actually where most of our customers are,” he said, while fully agentic deployments are at the “beginning of the adoption curve.” This approach lets customers ease into agentic, build confidence and move to fully autonomous at their own pace.

NiCE designed the product for that approach. An agent can serve as the orchestration layer, calling existing flows as tools. Flows can also be placed in front of agents, for example, to scrub credit card numbers or other personal data before any data reaches a model. Ho described the release as “an evolution, not a replacement,” with production deployments, application programming interfaces and integrations continuing to run unchanged.

That’s a meaningful advantage over AI-native challengers whose pitch effectively requires a rebuild. Contact centers are the fastest-moving environments, and deterministic workflows aren’t legacy baggage. They’re how a business enforces what a large language model shouldn’t be deciding.

“You can have the best builder experience, but if you don’t have any feedback loop on what you’re building, you’re never going to build a great agent,” Boutier said. The new tracing shows each turn: which skill loaded, which tool was called and with what arguments, and when the agent handed off to a flow.

The Simulator now supports multivariate testing of up to 10 variants, using an LLM-as-judge to run synthetic customers against an agent. Boutier ran the same agent on two models and found that one was faster and consumed fewer tokens. This shifts model selection from a preference to a data-backed economic decision.

Voice-to-voice support may be the first feature customers deploy. Boutier noted that buyers are open to using a speech-to-text and text-to-speech cascade, “but what they realize is that voice-to-voice models sound just better.” In the demo, the agent delegated tool calls to a separate model while continuing to talk, making the conversation sound far more natural.

Cognigy now serves as both a Model Context Protocol client and server and supports agent-to-agent connections, including one customer linking Cognigy to agents built with Microsoft’s tooling. NiCE is also co-developing the Personal Agent Protocol with Meta and Sierra, which isn’t live yet. Boutier described Cognigy as “the front door” of the contact center, where a consumer’s personal agent must authenticate before it can proceed. It’s great to see NiCE collaborating with Sierra, a direct competitor, on this, as it makes things easier for a customer.

The industry views agent identity as a shared responsibility. But as Sierra outlines, companies can also let personal agents work through their websites and APIs, so the front-door position depends on enterprises routing that traffic through Cognigy. This lets brands interact with personal agents safely.

There has been a wave of companies banning personal agents, which I think is a mistake. If something is good for a consumer, it will happen, so it’s better to be on the leading edge of enabling it rather than fighting it.

This release is less about new capabilities and more about NiCE betting on where value will accrue as AI agents mature. Intelligence is getting cheaper. Dependability, governance and the ability to blend autonomous reasoning with deterministic control are not.

NiCE is the market leader in contact center as a service, as Cognigy was in conversational AI. Now the challenge is to get an easier-to-work-with Cognigy into the hands of thousands of CXone customers without creating a sprawl of individually governed agents. This will allow NiCE to maintain its industry leadership as personal agents arrive. As it does that, the Cognigy acquisition will move from an add-on to a core component of the NiCE platform.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5461. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5460. Jackson's AMTC to Open State-of-the-Art ManuTech Prototyping Center

Lean Rocket Lab, JAMA and the Shop Rat Foundation will cut the ribbon Dec. 14, giving startups, manufacturers, students and apprentices a place to scan, design and build real parts

JACKSON, Mich., Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Startups and small to medium-sized manufacturers in the Jackson region will soon be able to go from idea to physical prototype in a single afternoon. The Advanced Manufacturing Training Center (AMTC) consortium, a partnership between the Lean Rocket Lab, Jackson Area Manufacturers Association (JAMA) and Shop Rat Foundation, will open its new ManuTech Prototyping Center with a ribbon cutting on Dec. 14, 2026.

The ribbon cutting anchors the ManuTech LIVE Innovation Experience 2026, a public event from 3:30-6 p.m. at the AMTC, 3517 Scheele Drive in Jackson. Attendees will see startups putting the new center to work and technology companies demonstrating their products on the AMTC's live factory floor.

The ManuTech Prototyping Center brings a complete digital-to-physical workflow under one roof for both physical products and electronic hardware. Users can capture an existing part, refine it as a digital model, and produce it in more than one material and process.

"The ManuTech Prototyping Center will connect digital design with physical production, allowing users to scan objects, develop digital models and produce parts using different manufacturing processes," said Brandon Marken, CEO of Lean Rocket Lab. "Manufacturers need places where they can explore new ideas, see technology in action and understand what's possible before taking the next step. This space will make those opportunities more accessible and give businesses a place to connect innovation with real-world manufacturing needs."

The Center's equipment includes a handheld 3D scanner to capture existing parts and objects as precise digital models; a large-format resin 3D printer for high-detail, smooth-finish prototypes; fused deposition modeling (FDM) 3D printers for fast, durable functional parts and test fixtures; and a computer-aided design workstation using SOLIDWORKS software, the industry-standard engineering software, to modify or design parts from scratch. Additional capabilities for electronics are also being added to the center's current capabilities in the near future.

Lean Rocket Lab leads the center, which is built primarily for startups and small to medium-sized manufacturers that need to test ideas without investing in equipment of their own. However, users won't be on their own: Lean Rocket Lab Entrepreneur-in-Residence Steve Tebbetts, who previously ran a prototyping lab for a Michigan OEM, will guide them through the product development process.

Because the center sits inside the AMTC, it also strengthens the training programs already housed there. JAMA apprentices and Shop Rat Foundation students will gain hands-on exposure to the same scanning, design and additive manufacturing tools that companies are adopting today.

"Manufacturing is changing, and our workforce needs opportunities to learn, adapt and grow alongside that change," said Olivia Steele, executive director of JAMA. "Events like ManuTech LIVE help people see the career possibilities in front of them and understand the role apprenticeship training can play in building a strong manufacturing workforce."

The Shop Rat Foundation, which reaches more than 4,000 young people each year, sees the center as a new entry point into technical careers.

"Getting our youth excited about how things work can open the door to opportunities they may never have considered," said Kelly Kofflin, executive director of the Shop Rat Foundation. "Bringing students, educators and industry together helps make those connections and shows young people that they can have a future in advanced manufacturing."

The ManuTech LIVE event will also feature select startups demonstrating technology and products designed to address practical business and industry challenges. Detect-It, will showcase artificial intelligence-powered vision technology for inspection and defect detection, with a potential demonstration involving parts produced on a CNC machine. Jendamark will demonstrate its Odin Workstation, an AI-powered manufacturing execution system designed for assembly processes. And Machine AI Solutions is expected to showcase technology related to machine data and monitoring.

Additional participating companies include Veriti, which offers a platform that converts 2D engineering drawings into quotes for machine shops; Tackboard, which provides digital maintenance ticketing software; Strain Guard, which makes a physical product designed for RV owners to help protect cables from damage; and Cerebion, which focuses on cybersecurity for industry.

In addition to the Prototypic Center launch, ManuTech LIVE will also feature real-time demonstrations of manufacturing technology within the broader AMTC facility, including a manual machining lab, a welding lab and multiple computer numerical control (CNC) machines. JAMA will also share information on its apprenticeship programs, and the Shop Rat Foundation will highlight its youth STEM programming.

ManuTech LIVE is designed for manufacturers, technology companies, students, educators, community leaders and anyone interested in the technologies and training shaping the region's manufacturing future.

To learn more about the event or to RSVP, visit www.go.leanrocketlab.org/events/manutech

About the AMTC consortiumThe Advanced Manufacturing Training Center (AMTC) in Jackson is operated through a partnership between the Jackson Area Manufacturers Association, the Shop Rat Foundation and Lean Rocket Lab. Together, the partners combine apprenticeship training, youth STEM education and startup and small business support in a single facility dedicated to the region's manufacturing future.

About Lean Rocket LabThe Lean Rocket Lab is a nonprofit organization focused on helping entrepreneurs, startups, and small businesses at every stage of growth. As a designated Michigan Economic Development Corporation (MEDC) Small Business Support Hub, the Lean Rocket Lab delivers practical tools, targeted resources, and hands-on support to help entrepreneurs and innovators move from idea to execution. For more information, please visit leanrocketlab.org.

About JAMAJackson Area Manufacturers Association (JAMA) is in the heart of manufacturing in Jackson County and beyond, with a statewide reach across Michigan. We bring together local manufacturers, educators, and industry experts to spark collaboration, fuel innovation and drive growth. Through our Advanced Manufacturing Training Center and apprenticeship programs, we equip students and professionals with the hands-on skills today's workforce demands. For more information, visit jacksonjama.org.

About The Shop Rat FoundationThe Shop Rat Foundation is a Jackson-based, nonprofit organization with a mission to "ignite interest in manufacturing and professional trades careers among youth through innovation and outreach." The organization's curriculum focuses on computer science, engineering, precision machining, robotics and welding, as well as construction trades; serving over 4,000 youth annually through in-school partnership programs, extracurricular classes and camps, as well as community events focused on opportunities for youth to gain awareness of, engage with and explore careers within the manufacturing and professional trades sectors. Learn more at www.shoprat.org.

#5458. WeFetch AI Corp. Is the New Name of GreenCore Solutions Corp.

gtinfetch.ai, WeFetch.ai's lead product, removes the guess from artificial intelligence (AI) shopping: the right barcode, and signed proof of it.

VANCOUVER, BC and LONDON, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- WeFetch AI Corp., the artificial intelligence (AI) shopping company formerly named GreenCore Solutions Corp., has completed its change of name. The Registrar of Companies for British Columbia issued the Certificate of Change of Name on November 13, 2026.

An AI agent picks a product in words. The same words can match a dozen barcodes: the right brand in the wrong size, last year's pack, a look-alike from another maker. When the agent guesses, the shopper gets the wrong product, the brand loses a sale it had already won, and the retailer pays for the return.

The Company's lead product, gtinfetch.ai, removes the guess. It answers for 84,810,515 barcodes from 376,271 makers across 3,520,471 points of sale. An AI agent sends a barcode and gets a firm answer: verified, not verified or unknown, with the sources behind it.

When an AI agent buys on a shopper's behalf, someone has to be able to show it bought the right product. Today nobody can: the agent's choice leaves no record. gtinfetch.ai gives the agent a signed receipt of the check, written at rco.wefetch.ai and open to public verification. The retailer, the brand and the auditor can each see what was checked, when, and what the answer was. The mark is "Barcode verified".

The full record now answers from France, Singapore and the United States. Every barcode also has its own free public page at gtinfetch.ai. The three regions are where AI shopping starts. Singapore has the highest consumer use of generative AI in Asia, at 64.3% of working-age people. France stands at 49.6% and the United States at 33.0%, against 18.8% worldwide. (Source: Microsoft AI Diffusion Report, Q2 2026.) They are also the home markets of the AI that shoppers ask: ChatGPT and Claude in the United States, Mistral in France, and Singapore among the top countries in the world for Claude use per head. (Source: Anthropic Economic Index.)

WeFetch.ai, the barcode fetch system for AI agents. It answers for 84 million products in 70 countries, with 3.5 million points of sale on its own record, and includes:

It is AI native, and works with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Mistral, Perplexity and Muse. Every answer is signed.

"Words were the first generation of AI answers. Barcodes are agentic commerce," said Matthew Keddy, Chief Executive Officer of WeFetch AI Corp. "Every AI agent that moves from search results to shopping needs barcode precision. wefetch has it, signed, in three regions."

The market: Gartner forecasts $2.7 trillion in AI spending in 2026. McKinsey projects that AI agents will orchestrate $3 trillion to $5 trillion in global commerce by 2030, up to $1 trillion of it in US retail. Every one of those AI agent purchases needs the right barcode.

WeFetch AI Corp. develops AI software products for AI shopping, retail, grocery and fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG). Its lead product, gtinfetch.ai, is the AI agentic shopping barcode engine: 84 million barcodes, answered for the agents of seven AI labs. WeFetch is headquartered in Vancouver, Canada, with sales offices in London, UK. Please visit: wefetch.ai

#5457. FAA grounds all domestic flights after reported network outage

The Federal Aviation Administration today grounded all domestic flights in the U.S.

The rare order was issued by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC. It’s an FAA facility in Northern Virginia that is responsible for monitoring air traffic and mitigating potential risks. When ATCSCC identifies issues such as airport congestion, it provides local officials with guidance on how to address them.

The ATCSCC sent today’s ground stop order to all 22 regional air traffic control centers in the U.S. The memo explained that the move was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy elaborated in a post on X that the FAA “issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

The post didn’t provide any details about the communication issue. According to CBS News, the problem affects a “private communications network” that connects components of the U.S. air traffic control system. The outlet cited sources as saying that an update caused the network to reboot, which in turn led it to crash.

On Tuesday, the FAA announced that it was expanding its use of an artificial intelligence system called SMART. The software analyzes weather patterns, flight paths and related data points to generate air traffic scheduling recommendations. The FAA says that the software is designed to reduce delays and fuel consumption.

The agency last issued a national ground stop in January 2023. It was a response to an issue in the FAA’s NOTAM system, which it uses to notify pilots about hazards such as closed runways. The shutdown lasted about two hours and grounded 9,500 flights.

The current shutdown is already much longer, having started at 3:54 p.m. EST. More than 13,000 flights have reportedly been delayed or canceled. Eurocontrol, an organization that helps European Union member states coordinate air traffic, suspended flights to the U.S. at the request of the FAA.

FAA officials said that inbound international flights will be “handled on a case by case basis.” American Airlines, meanwhile, stated that flights already airborne will proceed to their destinations. The airline reportedly expects the disruption to last all day.

#5454. Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain."

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis."

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks."

Why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

#5452. 10 milestones in Nvidia's growth, from the NV1 to $3 trillion in market value

Free daily briefing on global business news.

This Nvidia timeline traces 10 milestones in the chipmaker's rise, from its 1993 founding and GeForce graphics cards to CUDA, AI data centers and trillion-dollar market value

Nvidia $NVDA started in April 1993 in Santa Clara, California, as a company building 3D graphics for PCs. The founders were Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. On June 18, 2024, it overtook Microsoft $MSFT as the most valuable listed company. Company rankings by market value change daily. That makes the June 2024 milestone a dated one, not a permanent title. The two dates sit 31 years apart.

The link between those two dates is the graphics chip itself. Hardware designed to draw 3D scenes for games turned out to suit other kinds of computing work. Nvidia's CUDA software, introduced in 2006, let developers use its GPUs for general-purpose programs. In 2012, AlexNet showed that the same chips could speed up deep learning. Those two steps pointed the company toward AI systems for data centers. After OpenAI released ChatGPT in November 2022, demand for Nvidia's data center chips rose.

Not every step moved the company forward. Its first product, released in 1995, did not succeed commercially. The company changed its approach to graphics afterward. A planned acquisition was abandoned after regulators raised objections. Its purchase of Mellanox, by contrast, added data center networking technology. Those setbacks and deals sit in the timeline alongside product launches and market value figures.

This Nvidia timeline covers 10 milestones, from the 1993 founding to the June 2024 day the chipmaker passed Microsoft in market value. It is a selection, not a complete history of the company. The entries run in chronological order and are not ranked. The early entries cover graphics chips for PCs and a game console. The middle entries cover the software and research that opened GPUs to new uses. The later entries cover data center hardware, acquisitions, export restrictions and the market value steps that followed. Market value claims in the timeline are tied to the dates they occurred. Each entry stands on its own, with the date, product, deal or figure that defined it.

Nvidia $NVDA was founded in April 1993 by three co-founders: Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. The company was based in Santa Clara, California.

Its early work centered on 3D graphics for personal computers.

The NV1 was Nvidia $NVDA's first product, and it reached the market in 1995. It did not succeed commercially.

The chip arrived about two years after the company's founding. It was Nvidia's first attempt to sell graphics hardware to buyers.

That attempt did not catch on. The commercial failure led Nvidia to change its approach to graphics.

Nvidia $NVDA went public on Nasdaq $NDAQ on January 22, 1999, at $12 a share. In October of that year, it launched the GeForce 256 and marketed the chip as the first GPU, or graphics processing unit.

The listing came less than six years after the company's April 1993 founding. Once its shares began trading on Nasdaq, Nvidia became a publicly traded company.

The product milestone followed about nine months after the listing. In October 1999, Nvidia released the GeForce 256, a graphics chip for PCs.

Nvidia promoted the GeForce 256 as the first GPU. That label was the company's own marketing claim. Nvidia used the term to present the chip as a new kind of graphics product.

The two 1999 events differed in kind. The IPO changed how Nvidia was owned and financed. The GeForce 256 gave the company a new chip and a name for the category it claimed that chip started.

Nvidia $NVDA supplied the graphics processor for Microsoft $MSFT's original Xbox, the game console that launched in 2001. The deal added a console business to the chipmaker's existing sales of graphics cards for PCs.

With the Xbox, Nvidia's graphics hardware reached players through two kinds of products. One was a graphics card installed in a personal computer. The other was a home console sold under Microsoft's brand.

Nvidia $NVDA announced CUDA in November 2006. The platform lets developers run general-purpose programs on Nvidia GPUs, not only graphics code.

The announcement came alongside the GeForce 8800 GTX, a graphics card built on Nvidia's G80 chip. Nvidia introduced the software platform and the new card at the same time.

A GPU had been designed to render images for games. CUDA gave programmers a way to write software that put an Nvidia GPU to work on tasks other than drawing a picture on a screen. That widened the range of jobs the company's hardware could take on.

The GeForce 8800 GTX was a graphics card for PC gaming. Paired with CUDA, the launch addressed two audiences. One was buyers looking for a graphics card. The other was developers who wanted to use a GPU for their own programs.

CUDA's role grew in the years after 2006. It later became the software base for much of AI computing.

That later role traces back to the November 2006 announcement. It marked the point when Nvidia began offering its GPUs for general-purpose computing as well as for graphics.

AlexNet, a neural network built by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, won the 2012 ImageNet competition. The three researchers trained it on two Nvidia $NVDA GTX 580 GPUs.

AlexNet was a deep learning model. Its ImageNet result showed that GPUs could speed up that kind of work.

The 2012 win linked Nvidia's graphics processors to deep learning research. The link came through the work of Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, who chose a pair of the chipmaker's GPUs to train their network.

In April 2016, Nvidia $NVDA announced the Tesla $TSLA P100, a GPU built on its Pascal architecture. That same month, it introduced the DGX-1, an AI system. Together, the two launches marked the chipmaker's turn toward the data center.

The two products sat at different levels. The Tesla P100 was a single chip. The DGX-1 was a complete system built for AI work. With it, Nvidia offered a finished machine as well as the processors that go inside one.

In August 2016, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang delivered a DGX-1 to OpenAI. The handover came four months after the system's introduction. It put one of the new machines in the hands of an organization working on artificial intelligence.

Pascal did not stay Nvidia's newest design for long. In 2017, the GPU maker followed it with Volta, an architecture that added tensor cores.

Nvidia $NVDA agreed in March 2019 to buy Mellanox for $6.9 billion. The purchase closed in April 2020 and gave the chipmaker data center networking technology.

About 13 months passed between the announcement and the close. The deal took a business built around graphics processors into the networking side of the data center.

A much larger bid followed. In September 2020, five months after the Mellanox purchase closed, Nvidia announced a $40 billion deal to buy Arm.

That agreement never closed. It stayed pending for about 17 months. In February 2022, the companies abandoned it after regulators raised objections.

The two deals ended differently. Mellanox became part of Nvidia, and its networking technology stayed with the chipmaker. The Arm bid ended without Nvidia acquiring the company.

Nvidia $NVDA announced the H100, a data center GPU built on its Hopper architecture, in March 2022. Demand for Nvidia's data center chips rose after OpenAI released ChatGPT in November 2022.

Hopper is the name of the architecture. H100 is the name of the data center GPU built on it. Nvidia announced the chip in March, before ChatGPT reached the public that November.

ChatGPT was an OpenAI product, not an Nvidia one. The demand that rose after its release was for Nvidia's data center chips. The H100 belongs to that category.

U.S. export rules also limited where those chips could be sold. In October 2022, the U.S. imposed restrictions on exports of advanced chips to China. The rules covered the A100 and the H100, two of Nvidia's data center GPUs.

The H100 therefore came under U.S. export restrictions for China in the same year Nvidia announced it.

Nvidia followed Hopper with another architecture. In March 2024, the company announced Blackwell.

This stretch of Nvidia history runs from the H100 announcement in March 2022 to the Blackwell announcement in March 2024. The October 2022 export restrictions and the November 2022 release of ChatGPT fall between those two dates.

Nvidia $NVDA's market value first passed $1 trillion in May 2023. It crossed $2 trillion in February 2024 and $3 trillion in June 2024. On June 18, 2024, the chipmaker overtook Microsoft $MSFT as the most valuable listed company.

Market value, also called market capitalization, is a company's share price multiplied by its number of shares outstanding. It moves with the stock on every trading day. Each threshold records how investors priced Nvidia on a given date. It is not a fixed measure of the business.

Market value is also separate from a company's sales or profit. A higher market value does not mean a company sold more or earned more than another. It reflects the price investors paid for its shares, multiplied across all of them. When Nvidia passed Microsoft, the comparison was between two stock market valuations on the same day.

The word "listed" matters in that comparison. The ranking covers companies whose shares trade on public stock exchanges. A privately held company has no daily share price. It cannot be measured on the same daily basis.

The two trillion-dollar steps took different lengths of time. Nvidia needed about nine months to go from $1 trillion in May 2023 to $2 trillion in February 2024. The climb from $2 trillion to $3 trillion took about four months and ended in June 2024. Each step added the same $1 trillion in market value. The second step took less than half as long as the first.

The Microsoft milestone came in the same month as the $3 trillion crossing. The lead was a position held on a particular trading day. A company that ranks first on one day can fall behind on the next as share prices move.

The dates mark first crossings only. They show when Nvidia's value reached each level, not whether it stayed above that level afterward. Round numbers such as $1 trillion are reference points for share-price valuation. They are not figures the company reported in its earnings.

#5450. Innovative Immunology Biotech Windward Bio Lists on Nasdaq

SHANGHAI, Nov. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Windward Bio, a portfolio company of Qiming Venture Partners and a clinical-stage biotechnology company, successfully listed on Nasdaq on November 13, 2026. Windward Bio (Nasdaq: WWB) priced its IPO at $17.00 per share. Its shares closed at $28.50 on the first trading day, up 68% from the IPO price, giving the company a market capitalization of approximately $1.69 billion. This is Qiming Venture Partners' 11th IPO in 2026.

Qiming Venture Partners invested in Windward Bio's inaugural Series A financing in 2025 and continued to support the company in its Series B financing in 2026. Qiming also participated in this IPO financing round.

Windward Bio was founded in 2024 with a mission to transform the treatment paradigm for patients living with chronic inflammatory diseases through the development of differentiated biologic therapies targeting clinically validated disease pathways. Led by a team with extensive expertise across discovery, development, and commercialization, Windward Bio is advancing a pipeline of ultra-long-acting antibody medicines to improve clinical outcomes, reduce treatment burden and expand treatment options for patients with serious respiratory and dermatologic diseases, including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and atopic dermatitis.

Windward Bio's lead program, WIN378, is a potentially novel anti-TSLP monoclonal antibody engineered for improved potency and extended half-life. WIN378 is currently being evaluated in POLARIS-1, a Phase 2/3 study in severe uncontrolled asthma, and SIRIUS, a Phase 2 study in COPD. The company's pipeline also includes WIN027, a clinical-stage, long-acting bispecific antibody targeting TSLP and IL-13 with potential applications across multiple inflammatory and immunological diseases. Windward Bio holds exclusive global rights (excluding Greater China and certain Asian countries) to WIN378 through a licensing agreement with Kelun-Biotech and Harbour BioMed, and has separately licensed WIN027 from Qyuns Therapeutics.

"Qiming Venture Partners invests in differentiated, globally competitive biotech innovation designed to address significant unmet needs for patients, and Windward Bio exemplifies this approach. We believe novel, long-acting biologics will reshape the treatment of severe chronic respiratory and skin diseases, and that WIN378 and WIN027 have the potential to expand and meaningfully improve the treatment options available to patients. In the hands of Luca and his team, with their expertise and proven track record, Windward is well-positioned to deliver on this potential, and we look forward to supporting the company through its next phase of growth," said Alexander Sinclair Wilson, Principal at Qiming Venture Partners.

Qiming Venture Partners was founded in 2006. Currently, Qiming Venture Partners manages eleven US Dollar funds and seven RMB funds with $9.5 billion in capital raised. Since our establishment, we have invested in outstanding companies in the Technology and Healthcare industries at the early and growth stages.

Since our debut, we have backed over 630 fast-growing and innovative companies. Over 290 of our portfolio companies have achieved exits through IPOs at the NYSE, NASDAQ, HKEX, Shanghai Stock Exchange, or Shenzhen Stock Exchange, or through M&A or other means. There are also over 110 portfolio companies that have achieved unicorn or super unicorn status.

Many of our portfolio companies are today's most influential firms in their respective sectors, including Xiaomi, Meituan, Bilibili, Zhihu, Roborock, Hesai Technology, UBTech, WeRide, HyperStrong, Insta360, Unisound, Biren Technology, Z.AI, Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals, Tigermed, Zai Lab, CanSino Biologics, SchrÃ¶dinger, APT Medical, Sanyou Medical, AmoyDx, SinocellTech, Insilico Medicine, AusperBio, Yuanxin Technology, Medilink Therapeutics, LaNova Medicines, StepFun, among many others.

#5449. How much of the S&P 500 is Nvidia? It changes daily, and here is why

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How much of the S&P 500 is Nvidia depends on its market value, and Jensen Huang's chipmaker shows the concentration risk inside cap-weighted index funds

An S&P 500 index fund looks like a vote for 500 companies at once. The money inside it is not split evenly, though. Each dollar is divided according to company size. The largest firms take a far bigger slice than the smallest ones. Nvidia $NVDA shows how that design plays out at the top of the market.

The split is set by float-adjusted market capitalization, meaning the value of the shares available to public investors. A stock that outpaces the rest of the market gains weight automatically. No committee vote or rebalancing is needed to make that happen.

The chipmaker dates to 1993, when Jensen Huang founded it with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. Huang has run it as chief executive ever since. The company first passed a $4 trillion market value on July 9, 2025. On Oct. 29, 2025, it became the first public company to reach $5 trillion. A market value that large translates directly into a heavy presence in any cap-weighted index.

So how much of the S&P 500 is Nvidia? The answer changes every trading day. Its weight rises and falls with its share price relative to the rest of the roughly 500 companies in the index. Any precise percentage is a snapshot tied to a specific date. Index providers and fund companies publish dated holdings that show the current figure.

Concentration is the reason that weight matters. When a few stocks make up a large part of an index, the index's return depends heavily on how those few perform. A drop in one top holding moves the whole benchmark more than a drop in a smaller company would. Anyone who owns an S&P 500 fund holds those stocks automatically, whether or not they chose to.

The 10 slides that follow explain how index weights are calculated and why Nvidia's share keeps shifting. They trace the company's growth under Huang and look at how top-heavy the index has become. They compare the cap-weighted index with its equal-weight counterpart. They also revisit earlier periods when IBM $IBM, AT&T $T and technology stocks around the 2000 dot-com peak held outsized weight. The final slides cover what concentration risk means for index-fund investors, how to measure exposure and what could change Nvidia's weight.

The S&P 500 assigns each company a weight based on its float-adjusted market capitalization. Companies with more tradable market value take bigger slices of the index, and smaller companies take thinner ones.

Market capitalization is a company's share price multiplied by its shares outstanding. The float adjustment trims that share count to the stock available for public trading. Shares held by insiders, governments or other long-term strategic holders are generally excluded. S&P Dow Jones Indices, the company that maintains the index, applies this adjustment so each weight reflects stock that investors can actually buy.

The index did not always work this way. The S&P 500 launched in 1957 and was weighted by full market capitalization for decades. It switched to float adjustment in 2005, phasing the change in over that year.

Every constituent's weight is a share of one combined total. All the weights together add up to 100%. When one company gains weight, others must lose some.

Weights shift whenever prices move. A company whose stock rises faster than the rest of the index gains weight. A company whose shares lag loses weight in the same way. Neither change requires any trading by the index.

This self-adjusting design matters for index funds. A fund that holds each stock in proportion to its market value stays aligned with the index as prices change. It does not need to buy or sell shares just because one stock has outpaced another. Trading is mostly needed when companies join or leave the index, or when share counts change.

The S&P 500 is usually described as 500 companies, and it holds roughly that many. It lists slightly more than 500 tickers, though. Some companies have more than one share class in the index. Alphabet $GOOGL, for example, has both its Class A and Class C shares included.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average works on a different principle. It is price-weighted, so a stock with a higher share price counts for more, regardless of the company's total value. In the S&P 500, share price alone does not set a company's influence.

Stock splits show the difference. A split lowers a company's share price and raises its share count by the same factor. Its market value stays the same, so its S&P 500 weight does not change. In the Dow, the lower share price shrinks the stock's pull on the average.

A committee at S&P Dow Jones Indices decides which companies belong in the S&P 500. It applies eligibility rules covering U.S. domicile, liquidity and a record of positive earnings. Once a company is in, the market-cap formula sets its weight.

Nvidia $NVDA's weight in the S&P 500 has no fixed value. It equals the chipmaker's float-adjusted market value divided by the combined float-adjusted value of every company in the index, and both numbers shift with every trade. The result is a share that changes throughout every trading session.

That makes any answer to how much of the S&P 500 is Nvidia a reading from one particular moment. A figure quoted in a news story last month describes the index as it stood on that day. Prices may have moved enough since then to make it stale.

The weight responds to relative performance, not absolute performance. If Nvidia's stock climbs while most of the index stays flat, its slice grows. If Nvidia and the rest of the market rise by the same proportion, its weight stays where it was. A sharp single-day drop in Nvidia shrinks its share even if nothing else moves.

Moves in other large companies matter too. The index total includes every constituent, so a rally in other megacaps enlarges the denominator. Nvidia's weight can slip on a day when its own stock does nothing at all.

The most reliable way to check a current figure is a published holdings list with a date on it. S&P Dow Jones Indices, which runs the index, publishes fact sheets that list the largest constituents by weight. Exchange-traded funds that track the S&P 500 also post their holdings online. Examples include the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust, the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF and the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF. Many ETFs update those lists daily.

A fund's reported weight can differ slightly from the index's own figure. Funds hold small amounts of cash, and their records may reflect a different pricing time. Traditional mutual funds that track the index usually disclose holdings less often, and typically with a lag.

Reading the figure correctly also means checking its date and its source. Two articles citing different numbers for Nvidia's weight are not necessarily in conflict. They may simply describe the index on different days.

Nvidia's position in the index is an output of market prices, not a fixed allocation. It is recalculated continuously during trading hours as those prices change.

Nvidia $NVDA grew from a 1993 startup making graphics chips for personal computers into the first public company to reach a $5 trillion market value. It crossed that mark on Oct. 29, 2025. Its path ran from video games to the data centers that train artificial intelligence models.

The company, based in Santa Clara, California, built its early business on graphics processors. These chips render images for games and other visual software. Nvidia went public in 1999. That same year it introduced the GeForce 256, which it marketed as the world's first GPU, short for graphics processing unit.

The design of those chips shaped what came next. A graphics processor runs many simple calculations at once, a method called parallel processing. That structure suits workloads well beyond drawing pixels on a screen.

In 2006, Nvidia introduced CUDA, a software platform that lets programmers use its chips for general-purpose computing. Researchers began using the chips for scientific and technical work. In 2012, an image-recognition model called AlexNet was trained on Nvidia graphics cards. Its results helped push deep learning into the mainstream of AI research.

Training and running AI models became a major source of demand. Data-center operators bought Nvidia processors to power those systems. The stock market priced that demand into the company's value. Nvidia first passed a $4 trillion market value on July 9, 2025.

A stock split along the way did not change Nvidia's standing in the S&P 500. In June 2024, the company carried out a 10-for-1 split. Each existing share became 10 shares, and each share's price was divided by 10.

Nvidia's total market value stayed the same at the moment of the split. The S&P 500 weights companies by market value rather than share price. The split therefore left Nvidia's index weight untouched. That weight still moves only as Nvidia's value changes relative to the other constituents.

Share price matters more in a different benchmark. In November 2024, Nvidia joined the Dow Jones Industrial Average, replacing Intel $INTC. The Dow is price-weighted. A stock's per-share price, not its total value, sets its influence there.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia $NVDA in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, and he has been its chief executive since the company was founded. More than three decades later, the same person still runs a business that carries an outsized weight in the S&P 500.

Huang was born in Taiwan and studied electrical engineering at Oregon State University and Stanford University. Before Nvidia, he worked in chip design and management at LSI Logic and Advanced Micro Devices. Malachowsky and Priem were engineers who came from Sun Microsystems. The three built the company around graphics processing for personal computers and video games. Nvidia is headquartered in Santa Clara, California.

Nvidia's early bet was on dedicated graphics hardware. In 1999, the company went public and released the GeForce 256, which it marketed as the first graphics processing unit, or GPU. That product category became the core of Nvidia's business for years.

A later decision under Huang widened what those chips could do. In 2006, Nvidia introduced CUDA, a software platform that lets developers use GPUs for general-purpose computing, not just graphics. CUDA gave programmers a way to run large parallel calculations on Nvidia hardware. It later became widely used in machine learning and AI research.

Nvidia has never gone through a chief executive transition. The executive who led a graphics-chip startup in the 1990s also oversaw its push into data-center computing. That continuity means one leader oversaw the company's path from gaming graphics to CUDA to AI infrastructure.

Market milestones arrived well into Huang's tenure. In November 2024, Nvidia joined the Dow Jones Industrial Average, replacing Intel $INTC.

Huang's decisions shaped what Nvidia makes and sells. The market's valuation of that business, not the tenure of its chief executive, sets the company's share of the S&P 500. A founder-led company receives no extra index weight for its leadership.

The S&P 500 is top-heavy. A small group of very large companies, Nvidia $NVDA among them, accounts for an outsized share of the index's total value. Several hundred other members split the rest.

The gap between the top and the bottom of the index is wide. The smallest constituents are worth a tiny fraction of the largest. A single megacap can carry more weight than dozens of the index's smaller companies combined. On many days, the index's move tracks a handful of giant stocks more closely than it tracks the typical member.

Megacap is an informal label for companies valued in the hundreds of billions of dollars or more. In the S&P 500, that group includes Nvidia, Microsoft $MSFT, Apple $AAPL, Alphabet $GOOGL, Amazon $AMZN, Meta $META, Broadcom $AVGO and Tesla $TSLA. Investors often group seven of them — Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla — under the nickname the Magnificent Seven.

Sector labels can hide how much of this weight sits in technology-driven businesses. The Global Industry Classification Standard, maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices and MSCI, places Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple and Broadcom in information technology. Alphabet and Meta, then called Facebook, moved to communication services in a 2018 revision of the standard. Amazon and Tesla are classified as consumer discretionary. The information technology sector's weight alone therefore leaves out several of the index's biggest technology-driven companies.

Many of these companies also share a common driver. Nvidia sells the chips used to build artificial intelligence data centers. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta buy large volumes of that hardware for their cloud and AI operations. When views on AI spending shift, the stocks at the top of the index can rise or fall together.

Share classes add a wrinkle. Alphabet has two classes of stock in the index, Class A and Class C. Its full weight is the sum of both lines.

The combined share held by the largest names changes every trading day. S&P Dow Jones Indices publishes a fact sheet listing the index's top 10 constituents by weight, along with the date those figures apply to.

The S&P 500 Equal Weight Index holds the same companies as the standard S&P 500, but it gives each one an identical slice. Comparing the two versions shows how much the familiar index depends on its largest members, including Nvidia $NVDA.

In the standard index, a company's influence tracks its float-adjusted market value. The biggest firms carry far more weight than the smallest ones. A move in a single megacap stock can outweigh the combined moves of dozens of smaller constituents.

The equal-weight version removes that hierarchy. At each rebalance, every constituent receives the same allocation. Nvidia then counts for no more than the smallest company in the index. A gain of a given size in any one stock has about the same effect on the equal-weight index, whichever company posts it.

S&P Dow Jones Indices rebalances the equal-weight index quarterly. Between those dates, winners drift above the target and laggards drift below it. At each rebalance, the index trims the stocks that rose and adds to those that fell. Every holding returns to an equal share.

That process requires more trading than the cap-weighted version, which adjusts on its own as prices move. Funds that track the equal-weight index generally have higher turnover as a result.

The gap between the two indexes is a readout of market breadth. When the largest stocks outperform the rest, the cap-weighted S&P 500 pulls ahead. Those stocks drive most of its return. When the largest names lag, the equal-weight version tends to come out ahead. In that version, the typical company matters as much as the giants.

A wide, persistent gap in favor of the cap-weighted index points to a market led by a narrow group. A narrowing gap, or one that flips, indicates that gains are spreading to more of the index's members. Neither version is a forecast. Each measures the same market from a different angle.

The equal-weight index also tilts toward smaller companies by design. Relative to the standard index, it gives more room to sectors such as industrials, utilities and real estate. It gives less room to technology. That sector mix is one reason the two versions can diverge even when no single stock dominates.

For a reader trying to gauge Nvidia's footprint in the index, the comparison isolates the effect of company size. In the equal-weight index, Nvidia's share returns to the same level as every other constituent each quarter. In the cap-weighted index, its share is set by its market value. The distance between those two treatments is one measure of how concentrated the standard index has become.

Nvidia $NVDA is not the first company to carry outsized weight in the S&P 500. IBM $IBM and AT&T $T each held unusually large shares of the index in earlier decades. Technology stocks as a group made up a very large slice of it around the 2000 dot-com peak.

The S&P 500 in its current form launched in 1957. It has weighted companies by market value from the start. That design means the most valuable companies of any era have had the most influence on how the index moves.

IBM was a leading example for much of the postwar period. Its mainframe computers dominated corporate data processing in the 1960s and 1970s. As investors rewarded that position, IBM's market value grew large enough that its share price could shift the broader index on its own.

AT&T held a similar position as the parent of the Bell System, the regulated telephone network that served most of the U.S. Its weight was reshaped by antitrust law rather than by share-price moves. An antitrust settlement broke up the Bell System, effective Jan. 1, 1984. AT&T's local phone operations were split into seven regional companies. The value once held in a single stock was spread across several separate ones.

The 1960s and early 1970s also produced the "Nifty Fifty." This was a group of large, fast-growing companies that many investors treated as stocks to buy and hold at almost any price. Many of those shares fell sharply in the 1973-74 bear market.

The late-1990s run-up created a different kind of concentration. Instead of one or two companies, an entire sector swelled. Microsoft $MSFT, Cisco $CSCO Systems, Intel $INTC and Oracle $ORCL were among the largest constituents as software, chip and networking stocks climbed. After the market peaked in March 2000, the sector's slide pulled the whole index down with it. The S&P 500 did not reach its low until October 2002.

Each episode unwound in its own way — a court-supervised breakup for AT&T, a prolonged market decline for the dot-com leaders. Intel, one of the largest companies of that era, was later replaced by Nvidia in the Dow Jones Industrial Average in November 2024. In the S&P 500, the mechanism has stayed the same throughout. The companies the market values most at a given moment carry the most weight, and the index rises and falls with them.

Concentration risk means an S&P 500 index fund's return depends heavily on a small number of very large stocks, including Nvidia $NVDA. A drop in one of those top holdings pulls the fund down further than it would if every company carried equal weight.

The cause is built into the fund's design. A fund that tracks the S&P 500 copies the index's weights, and those weights follow company size. A shareholder in that fund does not choose how much Nvidia to own. The index sets that amount, and the fund follows it.

This works in both directions. A rally in the largest stocks can lift the whole index even when many of its members are flat or falling. A selloff in the same names can pull the index down while many smaller companies hold steady. In either case, the headline index return reflects a handful of giants more than it reflects the typical company in the index.

Holders can also own more of a single company than they realize. An S&P 500 fund already includes Nvidia at its full index weight. An investor who also buys Nvidia shares directly adds to that position on top of the fund's holding.

The same overlap appears in other common funds. Nvidia is classified in the information technology sector. A fund tracking that sector therefore holds it too. Nvidia trades on the Nasdaq $NDAQ and is part of the Nasdaq-100, so funds tracking that index carry it as well. Nvidia has also been a member of the Dow Jones Industrial Average since November 2024, when it replaced Intel $INTC. Funds that track the Dow hold it for that reason.

Each of these holdings can look separate on an account statement. Underneath, several of them rest on the same company's share price.

Concentration can also tie the index to a single business trend. Nvidia sells chips used in data centers for artificial intelligence. Other large constituents, such as Microsoft $MSFT, Alphabet $GOOGL and Amazon $AMZN, run cloud computing businesses that operate those data centers. A shift in spending on that technology can move several of the biggest index members at once.

Concentration risk does not mean an index fund holds fewer companies. The fund still owns roughly 500 businesses across every sector of the index. What changes is how much each one counts toward the fund's daily gain or loss.

To measure Nvidia $NVDA exposure, an investor can check each fund's published holdings, multiply Nvidia's listed weight by the dollars held in that fund, and add any shares owned directly. Common ways to reduce that concentration include equal-weight index funds and spreading money across more sectors, company sizes and countries.

The holdings disclosure is the starting point. Most exchange-traded funds post their full portfolios on their sponsors' websites every trading day. Mutual funds report holdings less often. Their published weights can therefore lag the market.

A fund's holdings page lists Nvidia as a percentage of the fund's assets. Applying that percentage to the dollar value of the position gives the amount of Nvidia inside that fund. Repeating the step for every fund and adding directly owned shares produces a total. Dividing that total by the whole portfolio's value shows Nvidia's share of it.

Overlap is where totals often grow. Nvidia appears in S&P 500 funds, total U.S. stock market funds, Nasdaq $NDAQ-100 funds, large-cap growth funds, technology sector funds and semiconductor funds. It has also been part of the Dow Jones Industrial Average since November 2024, when it replaced Intel $INTC. An investor holding several of these products can own the same company many times over without buying it by name.

Many brokerages and fund research platforms offer portfolio analysis tools. These tools combine holdings across accounts and display the largest underlying positions in a single view.

On the reduction side, a fund tracking the S&P 500 Equal Weight Index gives Nvidia the same slice as every other constituent at each rebalance. That index rebalances quarterly. Between those dates, weights drift as prices move.

The equal-weight approach carries its own trade-offs. It leans toward smaller companies relative to the standard index. It also trades more often to restore equal weights.

Broader diversification is the other common method. Small-cap and mid-cap funds, international stock funds and sector funds outside technology hold little or no Nvidia. Adding them lowers the chip designer's share of a total portfolio without selling anything.

Selling existing positions is a further option, and it has consequences. In a taxable account, selling shares that have gained value can trigger capital gains tax. Shifting money inside tax-advantaged retirement accounts generally does not create an immediate tax bill.

Four forces move Nvidia $NVDA's weight in the S&P 500: its stock's performance against the rest of the market, the value of every other constituent, its share count and the portion of its shares counted as float. Each one acts on either Nvidia's own value or the index total.

Relative performance is the most direct driver. If Nvidia's stock gains more than the index as a whole, its slice grows. If it lags, its slice shrinks. That can happen even when the stock rises in absolute terms. A day when Nvidia climbs a little while other large stocks climb more can leave its weight lower than before.

The rest of the index matters too. The S&P 500 includes other megacap companies, among them Apple $AAPL, Microsoft $MSFT, Alphabet $GOOGL and Amazon $AMZN. A strong run in those stocks enlarges the index's total value. That pulls down Nvidia's share without any change in Nvidia's own market value. A broad rally across smaller constituents works the same way. It takes many more of them moving together to shift the total by a comparable amount.

Membership changes also alter the total. When the index committee replaces one company with another, the incoming firm's value takes the place of the outgoing firm's. Every other weight, including Nvidia's, adjusts slightly as a result.

Share count is another lever. Market capitalization equals the share price multiplied by the number of shares. Buybacks reduce that number, and new stock issuance increases it. Either one can move a company's value and its weight.

The float adjustment adds a further layer. S&P Dow Jones Indices, which maintains the S&P 500, counts only the shares available to public investors. Stock held by insiders or strategic holders can be excluded. A change in how many shares qualify as float can nudge a weight up or down.

A stock split is not one of these levers. It multiplies the share count and divides the price by the same factor, leaving market value and weight unchanged.

The S&P 500 also sets no ceiling on a single company's weight. Some capped indexes limit any one stock's share, but the flagship index lets weights follow market value.

The committee that oversees the S&P 500 chooses which companies belong, using criteria such as size, liquidity and profitability. It does not decide how much of the index each member gets. Once a company is in, its weight is mechanical. A change in Nvidia's weight reflects how investors value the company against roughly 500 others.
