#5439. 15 Years Ago, a Family Celebration Helped Two Sisters Notice a Gap in the Beauty Industry. Here’s How the Moment Sparked a 7-Figure Business.

Blushington co-CEOs Stephi Cohen and Nicki Maron reveal how they turned a standalone store into a growing franchise.

Fifteen years ago, Stephi Cohen and Nicki Maron encountered a common problem. The two sisters were getting ready for a special event, their younger sister’s bat mitzvah, and their family had all come over. Their house was packed, and they couldn’t afford to have a makeup artist and hair stylist cater to everyone.

“We started to think, well, you can go to Drybar and get your hair done,” Cohen says in a new interview with Entrepreneur. “But where can we go to get our makeup done?”

That’s where their “aha” moment happened. They thought that there should be a makeup place similar to Drybar but expanded, where customers could go to get their hair, makeup and skincare done, without having to pay the high price of a professional makeup artist coming to their homes.

Cohen called the business Blushington. She was just 21 years old at the time. Maron, her older sister, was 23 years old at the time and helped behind the scenes while pursuing a television career. She eventually joined the business full-time.

Today, the sisters are co-CEOs of Blushington, a company they report has a seven-figure run rate. Getting there meant rebuilding around a franchise model after temporarily closing their doors due to the pandemic.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and concision.

Stephi, what were you doing before you started Blushington?

Stephi Cohen: I went to the University of Arizona and studied a combination of communications and retail. I studied abroad in London and graduated early because I was ready to start my career. I always loved beauty and fashion — I have three sisters, and I was the one who was especially interested in that world. So, I worked in retail, but when I graduated, I wasn’t sure exactly what I wanted to do. I knew I wanted to be my own boss.

Nicki Maron: I was working in television marketing as Bill Lawrence’s assistant on Cougar Town. Working for him taught me about the power of grassroots marketing. While Stephi was developing the idea, I was helping her behind the scenes. Eventually, I realized I was probably spending more time working with her than working for Bill, and that wasn’t right. I needed to make the jump.

Also, I was thinking about how we could introduce the business to people who regularly needed their makeup done, including actresses like Courteney Cox. I was entrepreneurial, and I saw the same need Stephi saw: People didn’t have access to quality makeup applications at an affordable price.

What did you want customers to feel when they walked in?

Maron: We watched Pretty Woman as kids, and that scene where she’s treated badly in the store stayed with us. We wanted Blushington to be the opposite of that. There wasn’t a place where different generations of women could get their makeup done and feel that the artists were really listening to them. That was a big part of what we wanted to create.

Cohen: Nicki was there from the beginning, even when she had another job. She helped with everything. Having someone I trusted so much made a huge difference.

Where did the name Blushington come from?

Cohen: I had just come back from studying abroad in London. I liked names like Lexington and Kensington, but other names I considered were already trademarked. I wanted something that felt international, even though it was really two girls in Los Angeles. We combined “blush” with that kind of ending and came up with Blushington. Nobody had the name, so we could trademark it. Almost everybody in the family disliked it at first.

Maron: Myself included. I didn’t understand it. I give Stephi a lot of credit for trusting her instincts. If it had been up to me, we probably wouldn’t have gone with Blushington, and that would have been a mistake.

How did you find out whether other people shared your frustration?

Maron: We listened to friends and family. It wasn’t just us. It was our cousins, aunts, grandmothers and friends coming into town. There wasn’t a place that put service first in the way we wanted. The stores were modeled after our mom’s vanity. We wanted them to feel like a home away from home. We say that walking into Blushington should feel like a warm hug.

Stephi also believed makeup didn’t have to be reserved for weddings, prom or other special occasions. We launched services like Eyes Only for people who didn’t want a full face of makeup but still wanted to look and feel good.

What were the first concrete steps you took to get the business started?

Cohen: First, I asked people what they thought of the concept and tried to get their buy-in. Then I worked on a business plan. After that, we started looking for a location. I was driving down Sunset, near Drybar, and saw a “For Lease” sign. I thought, “This is a sign — I have to call.”

The space was a little bigger than we originally wanted, but it worked out well. From there, we needed architects and had to figure out the buildout. You learn as you go, and you surround yourself with people who have more experience than you do. For me, creating the space was the most exciting part. Then came finding the brands and sticking to our approach to product selection.

Cohen: We weren’t going to buy an entire product line just to carry a brand, and we still don’t. At the time, bigger brands often required you to meet a minimum or bring in the full line. We pushed back. We wanted to choose the products that made sense for our artists and customers.

Cohen: We brought together a board and a few investors who helped fund the buildout and the start of the business.

The pitch was that nobody was doing what we wanted to do. Investors could see the demand for blowout bars, and we were showing them a similar opportunity for makeup applications. Our product selection, artistry, pricing and overall model helped make the case.

Maron: You call everyone you know. You say, “This is what I’m doing. I need to find the right people to help me, and let’s do it together.”

Cohen: We talked to friends and family and kept getting the word out. Eventually, publicity helped bring people to us, rather than us always having to look for them. But in the beginning, we pounded the pavement.

How did you get your first paying customers?

Cohen: When we opened in 2011, Drybar was right next door. We had a great relationship, and people getting their hair done would come to us afterward for makeup. That helped introduce the business. We still believe in getting out into the community. Sometimes that means literally standing on the street and handing out cards. Nicki will do that herself.

Location matters, too. We want to be near complementary businesses — fitness, wellness and other places our customers already visit. Someone might finish a workout and come to us for a blowout.

Who did you imagine your typical customer would be?

Maron: The women who were in the room for our sister’s bat mitzvah. Someone like me who didn’t know much about makeup, someone like Stephi, who knew a lot, our mom and our grandmother.

I was a college soccer player. I didn’t wear makeup. Stephi would do my makeup, and our younger sister would do our hair.

That customer hasn’t really changed. She’s multigenerational. A mom comes in, and then her daughter comes in.

Cohen: We wanted to change the idea that getting your makeup done was only for a special occasion.

I had very bad acne in high school, and I understood what makeup could do for my confidence. I wanted to bring that experience to our customers.

It could be for a date, or it could simply be because you want to feel good about yourself. Keeping services affordable makes it easier for customers to come in more often, rather than only for a big event.

Maron: That remains part of our approach. You can get hair and makeup done under one roof for less than $200.

Maron: We signed a flagship space in New York City on March 11. On March 13, we closed our doors. It was one of the worst days of our lives. We had spent years building this family business, putting our hearts into it. We had to close all our locations and let our team go. Then we had to ask ourselves whether we should keep going at all.

Cohen: Not being able to provide income for our employees was one of the hardest parts. Before we could even figure out what we were going to do, we were worrying about them. We had to decide: Do we close the business, or can we come out of this stronger? Ultimately, we felt the franchise model was the best model for us.

Maron: During the pandemic, we created an online Blushington Academy. We certified artists across more than 40 states, and we have more than 250 artists in our portal. We wanted to support artists when people weren’t getting their hair and makeup done and we also saw more people wanting to become their own bosses. Franchising made sense because Stephi and I live in Los Angeles. Someone who lives in another city knows that community better than we do.

Maron: We have one corporate location in New York City and two open franchise locations in Boca Raton and Houston. Both franchisees were customers first. Karen, our first franchisee, had visited our Dallas and New York locations. Courtney, our Houston franchisee, had been emailing us about franchising since 2015.

Why would someone choose a Blushington franchise instead of starting an independent business?

Maron: Running a business on your own is difficult. In a franchise system, you have support. Our franchisees have Stephi, me and our team. We can help with real estate selection, marketing and operations because we’ve spent years learning how those things work. We also believe in the combination of blowouts, makeup and skincare in one appointment. Customers save time, and franchisees are working with an established concept and brand.

What affects the cost of opening a location?

Cohen: The investment includes the buildout, inventory and the products we select. We offer incentives for veterans and multi-unit owners. Our lounges also aren’t just service spaces. We host private parties and rent out the space, so that influences how we design and build them.

What did you need to demonstrate before asking someone to invest in a franchise?

Maron: We needed to show that customers wanted multiple services under one roof. We’re seeing close to two services per appointment. Someone comes in for a blowout and adds makeup or lashes. People don’t want appointments in different locations, long waits, inconsistent quality or an overwhelming product selection. Our business is built around making that easier.

#5438. Scott Bessent says Treasury wanted to blacklist Megaspeed ‘for months,’ blaming Howard Lutnick as Nvidia fallout widens: ‘Commerce has the pen’

Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick is now facing public pressure from his fellow Cabinet members over his decision to not blacklist Megaspeed, the cloud computing company at the center of Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

The Treasury Department, among other federal agencies, were in favor of placing trade restrictions on Megaspeed, but the decision ultimately lay with Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on Friday.

“There was coordination. Treasury, War, USTR, and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” he said. “But Commerce has the pen….You will have to ask them about their internal processes.”

Megaspeed is under investigation by the Justice Department over the suspected violation of U.S. export controls, which prohibit certain U.S.-made chips from being sold and shipped to China. Helmed by Alice Huang, the alleged spy, Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatric shipped at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to China over two years, The Information reported.

Lutnick is facing intensifying scrutiny over reports he took action to protect Nvidia from the Trump administration’s export controls of U.S. AI hardware to China. The commerce secretary reportedly spent months “undoing” efforts to hold Megaspeed accountable for potential export control violations, Axios reported. Bessent confronted Lutnick in the Situation Room following the midterm elections over not placing Megaspeed on the entity list, according to the outlet.

Bessent told CNBC, “We don’t repeat conversations in the Situation Room.”

According to the New York Times, when Trump officials approached Oracle about cancelling a $7 billion deal to lease chips to Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent, Lutnick’s top deputy Jeff Kessler spoke up and said Lutnick had issues with a cancellation, as it would halt the shipment of 100,000 advanced Nvidia AI chips. Lutnick reportedly said he didn’t understand the rush to scrap the deal.

The Commerce Department and Nvidia did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers want to hold Lutnick accountable for not placing Megaspeed on the blacklist.

“The obvious question is why did he choose to sell advanced chips?” Republican Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy told Politico. “Secretary Lutnick needs to answer that in front of God and country.”

Lutnick agreed to testify alongside Huang before the Senate Banking Committee to address national security concerns on Dec. 10.

Meanwhile, senior White House officials are now weighing whether to oust the commerce secretary from his position, Reuters reported. Even before news of Huang’s affair broke, Lutnick’s decision not to add 100 companies, including China’s DeekSeek, to the entity list put him in hot water.

Lutnick argued with senior White House officials that export regulations against China would stoke the trade war with China and he insisted on having conversations with Trump about China’s restricted access to U.S. chips, the Times reported.

The commerce secretary also had a friendly relationship and financial ties with Nvidia, bolstering concerns about favoritism toward the tech company.

“Howard is the person I talk to most in the administration—he’s on top of the technology and learning the industry quickly,” Huang said in September 2025.

Before Lutnick became commerce secretary, he was the CEO and chairman of investment bank Cantor Fitzgerald, which held about $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock prior to President Donald Trump’s second term.

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5437. Binance’s $6.3B Hack Fix Is Coming Tomorrow: Why the ZK Math Doesn't Tell the Whole Story

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance says the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

#5436. From paper routes to fighter jets: Shield AI’s bet on Seattle is a homecoming for its co-founders

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 9, 2026 at 6:36 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:36 am

As a kid on Mercer Island, Brandon Tseng delivered The Seattle Times and the Mercer Island Reporter for extra cash. Now he and his older brother, Ryan Tseng, are making news of their own in the Seattle region.

Shield AI, the San Diego defense tech company the brothers co-founded in 2015, announced a deal last week to buy Kirkland, Wash.-based radar maker Echodyne for up to $5.3 billion. Shield, now valued at $28.8 billion, had already unveiled plans in September to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet at a factory south of Seattle.

“I believe we will become one of the largest, or at least the fastest-growing employer in this region over the next several years,” Brandon Tseng said in an interview with GeekWire in the hours after the Echodyne acquisition was announced.

The company projects that it will employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle area by the early 2030s. It estimates the X-BAT could support about 8,000 jobs across the region in all, including jobs at Shield and its suppliers, according to an economic analysis drawing on company figures.

Tseng said Shield expects to have “well north of a million square feet” in the area before long, up from its initial 420,000-square-foot facility in Des Moines, Wash.

“That will really just be the beginning,” he said.

Brandon Tseng said the biggest reason Shield chose the Pacific Northwest for X-BAT production was the region’s “density of engineering and manufacturing talent,” pointing to Boeing, Microsoft and Amazon.

Inside the Echodyne deal: Shield believes the defense tech companies that succeed will need products that “sense, think, and act,” Tseng said. Its Hivemind autonomy software handles the thinking, and its V-BAT drone and X-BAT jet will handle the acting.

Echodyne becomes “the cornerstone of the sensing piece,” he said.

Tseng said Shield got a closer look at the market for sensors when it bought Australian optics company Sentient Vision Systems in 2024. That led the company to start looking seriously at other sensor makers, and eventually to Echodyne.

Shield and Echodyne had first crossed paths in 2016, when both were fledgling companies in the Department of Homeland Security’s Silicon Valley Innovation Program.

Nearly a decade later, the two companies’ teams were talking about working together when Echodyne began exploring a sale, Tseng said. The deal came together over several months. Tseng was at Echodyne the day it was announced last week, as the companies held all-hands meetings with their teams.

It’s an unusual deal: one venture-backed startup buying another, funded in part by a new venture round. Shield is raising $2.5 billion to help pay for the deal, including $1 billion in new funding at the $28.8 billion valuation — more than double what it was worth in March.

Echodyne has about 400 employees, after opening a $40 million radar factory in Woodinville in July. No layoffs are planned, the companies said. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will stay in that role, reporting to Shield CEO Gary Steele. The combined company will have about 2,700 employees.

The deal is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approval. Tseng said Shield plans a light touch for roughly the first year after that. Echodyne will keep selling radar to other manufacturers, many of them in counter-drone systems, while pursuing performance targets that could add $500 million to the price.

Deeper product integrations will be announced later, he said.

“They’ve been on a tear growth-wise, and we don’t want to get in their way,” Tseng said. “We don’t want to slow them down. We just want to supercharge them.”

He called the two companies’ cultures a strong match, describing both as mission-oriented and engineering-first. Echodyne’s best-selling radar, EchoShield, is designed to protect U.S. and allied service members from incoming drones.

Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders.

Tim Porter, the Madrona Venture Group managing director who has served on Echodyne’s board since 2014, called the deal another sign of the defense tech industry’s rapid growth in the Pacific Northwest.

Echodyne “rarely, if ever, showed up on lists of the hottest defense tech companies,” he wrote. Now it’s “under the radar no longer.”

X-BAT bet: Much of Shield’s growth in the region depends on an aircraft that hasn’t flown yet. Shield unveiled its first full-scale X-BAT prototype this month and shipped it to Kansas for flight testing, with first flight targeted by the end of the year. Shield has said low-rate production will start in Des Moines in mid-2027, with the first locally built jet due in early 2028.

The Pentagon and Shield have committed a combined $400 million to X-BAT’s development, but Shield hasn’t announced any production orders.

Ryan Tseng, speaking to Breaking Defense on the sidelines of the International Fighter Conference in Munich last week, said Shield expects to announce European X-BAT orders and partnerships but declined to discuss quantities, saying only, “Watch this space.” Andrew Hawkes, Shield’s X-BAT director for Europe, told Breaking Defense the company has “several active” sales campaigns there but declined to name customers.

Asked about the X-BAT schedule in the interview last week, Brandon Tseng acknowledged the challenge but pointed to the engineering and manufacturing teams that brought the prototype together in about a year. “There was no quit in them,” he said.

“It’s hard as hell, right? Just to move out on production that fast, but you have to be confident,” he said. “I’m confident.”

Tseng, a Naval Academy graduate who deployed twice to Afghanistan as a Navy SEAL, compared Shield’s pace to that experience, when small, mission-driven groups with the right tools and resources would “do things that people didn’t think were possible.”

Ryan Tseng, an electrical engineer, previously founded wireless charging company WiPower, which was acquired by Qualcomm. The brothers started Shield with Andrew Reiter, Shield’s first CTO, who returned to the company this year.

Seattle roots: The Tseng brothers and their sister grew up on Mercer Island. Brandon Tseng spent summers swimming in Lake Washington and played water polo for Mercer Island. Ryan Tseng, who was Shield’s CEO for about a decade, graduated from Mercer Island High School, and their sister graduated from the University of Washington.

Their father, Carlos Tseng, was CEO of Seattle-based Foss Maritime from 1996 to 2001, according to Tseng and Shield. He would stop at Pike Place Market on the way home from work, and the family “probably ate salmon every other day,” Brandon Tseng said.

The family moved to Florida in 2001. None of the Tsengs live in the area anymore, but Brandon Tseng still has friends here from middle school and high school and stops by Mercer Island when he has time on his visits to the region.

Shield’s Washington state connections go further. Steele, the company’s CEO since May 2025, grew up in Yakima and graduated from Washington State University.

Brandon Tseng called Shield’s expansion in the region “a fun homecoming” for him, his brother and Steele. He is based in Washington, D.C., but expects to spend more and more time in the Seattle area.

Tseng delivered the Times, then the afternoon paper, seven days a week from age 10 to 14, making his rounds every day after school and on weekends. He credits those routes with teaching him about hard work.

“It’s always felt like home,” he said. “It’s great to be back here.”

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5435. Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team as its general models start running robots

OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team, moving its researchers onto other teams.The company confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune. A company spokesperson said that robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision and portrayed the reorganization as a sign of the company’s commitment to robotics, rather than a retreat from it.OpenAI said it has reassigned its robotics research team to the company’s main research team, reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams have been reassigned to the company’s larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman.The change came recently enough that OpenAI had already registered a booth at CoRL, a top academic robotics conference in Austin, this week. Though the conference app and floor plan marked OpenAI’s spot, when Fortune visited booth #208, it sat empty with OpenAI’s logo nowhere to be seen.

OpenAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI)—the human-like AI that has been OpenAI’s goal since its founding—through other methods. In particular, OpenAI became increasingly devoted to training ultra-large language models on vast datasets of human-written text. This is the approach that eventually yielded the company’s breakthrough product ChatGPT in late 2022.OpenAI rebuilt a stand alone robotics team in 2024, announcing a partnership with the startup Figure to develop AI models for humanoid robots. That partnership ended in February 2025, when Figure said it would develop its own robot AI. OpenAI has said it is currently developing its own humanoid robot, with CEO Sam Altman targeting a first public demonstration in 2027. The company spokesperson said that despite the reorganization, OpenAI remains committed to bringing general-purpose robots into the world.The reorganization reflects a bet that is gaining traction across the AI industry: that general-purpose models built for language, code, and vision can also be used for “embodied AI”—where AI models control devices that can act in the physical world, such as robots, driverless cars, or drones. This would obviate the need to have separate robotics teams building specialized AI models just to be the digital “brains” for robots.Researchers have seen surprising performance when connecting GPT-6 Astra to robots, directly using the general-purpose AI model to perform some robotic tasks.Guanya Shi, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, reacted to the change at OpenAI, telling Fortune that he would interpret the move as a signal that OpenAI sees robotics as “no longer a special problem.” Instead, he said, they likely see robotics as a challenge that can be addressed as a downstream application of general intelligence—similar to the way the same underlying frontier AI models now power specialized coding tools, or tools for legal or financial work.OpenAI seemed to confirm this view in its response to Fortune. It said that at the start of the year, the company’s researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on AI models such as Sora, a video generation model that, in order to create realistic videos, had to have some implicit understanding of how the physical world works.But since then, the company spokesperson said, the company’s general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown that can be directly applied to robotics. This discovery is what motivated OpenAI to disband the stand alone robotics team and move the affiliated researchers onto teams working on more general AI models.The reorganization also comes at a time when OpenAI is under pressure to rein in its costs and show that it is more focused on a few, core products. Last year, Altman told the company that it needed to abandon “side quests,” and the company has jettisoned some efforts—including Sora—in order to reallocate computing resources to more core and potentially-profitable endeavors. The company is under pressure to stanch its heavy operating losses—which reportedly totaled $10.9 billion in the most recent quarter—as it seeks to close a new funding round and prepares for a possible IPO in early 2027.

This line of thinking—that general AI models can be applied directly to controlling robots without the need to create specialized models with “spatial intelligence”—would seem to challenge the assumptions underpinning many of today’s robotics startups, which have raised billions on the premise that robots need brains of their own.

But Russ Tedrake, an MIT professor and cofounder and CEO of Walden Robotics, said robotics companies still have an advantage the AI labs don’t: Their robots are already gaining work experience in real places, such as on factory floors. Such “deployment” experience—and the data these robots gather—helps robots adapt to specific workplaces and tasks. Better foundational models make that site-specific data more valuable because robots can learn from it faster, Tedrake said.

Recent experiments have tested how much work a general-purpose model can do without specialized training on robotic data. Researchers gave Astra camera images, robot information and a control interface that allowed the model to command the robot to take certain actions. In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark—where the model commands a simulated robot in a digital simulation, as opposed to a real robot—compared with 51.0% reported by the best specialized robotic models on this leaderboard.

Shi said advances in general models’ spatial and reasoning capabilities already let them handle tasks that previously required dedicated training. They can cope when a bottle is in a different position or the lighting changes, and reason about the sequence of a task or which step went wrong, he said.

Meanwhile, large language models are powerful but slow and need to be hosted in the cloud, meaning the robot or device needs a constant network connection. Shi still sees a need for smaller, specialized models that can run on a robot’s onboard computer without needing a constant internet connection.

“There may be different starting points for how to grow intelligence,” Pete Florence, cofounder of Generalist, a startup training general-purpose AI models for robots, told Fortune. He said it was unclear that any existing model would be the one that dominates robotics in the long-run.For its part, OpenAI said it was reassigning its robotics researchers to other teams because it now believes this is the best way to accelerate progress towards building general-purpose robots.

Back at booth #208 at CoRL, a few former members of the once-unified, stand-alone OpenAI robotics team milled about. They still drew a crowd, despite having no display or demo. After all, one of the conference’s hottest questions was how much robotics expertise would remain valuable as general-purpose models grew more capable—and the experience of those former OpenAI robotics researchers, now dispatched to other teams, offered one answer. Update, Nov. 13: This story has been updated to clarify the status of the OpenAI robotics team members who were at CoRL.

Wen Shao is a reporting fellow at Fortune covering AI, with a focus on the companies, economics, and infrastructure shaping the industry.

#5434. New tax incentives give Washington’s sustainable aviation fuel industry a boost

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 9, 2026 at 9:38 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Washington has cleared a milestone in its effort to become a hub for lower-carbon jet fuel, unlocking tax incentives aimed at attracting production to the state.

Gov. Bob Ferguson announced Friday that Washington has reached the capacity to produce at least 20 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually. That triggers incentives taking effect Jan. 1, including a tax credit starting at $1 per gallon for qualifying fuel. The credit rises to as much as $2 for fuels with greater emissions reductions.

The Department of Ecology recently surveyed potential producers and confirmed that Phillips 66’s Ferndale refinery alone has enough capacity to meet the threshold. The benchmark measures production capacity, not actual output.

Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is widely seen as one of the most promising near-term options for cutting aviation’s carbon emissions because it can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used in existing aircraft. But it remains more expensive than petroleum-based fuel, and production is orders of magnitude below the industry’s needs.

“We have so many unique assets in Washington that position us to be global leaders in the SAF transition, and this tax incentive is the final element needed to really unleash the tidal wave of opportunity,” said Jake Gentry, executive director of the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator, in a GeekWire interview.

The accelerator launched in January, bringing together airlines, SAF producers, public officials, researchers and others to promote the industry in the Pacific Northwest. Its work includes helping producers secure financing, develop feedstock supplies and connect with customers.

SAF can be produced from used cooking oil, grease and fats, plants and agricultural waste, and captured carbon. Its climate benefits depend on the raw materials and energy used to make it.

The fuel still produces carbon dioxide when burned. But unlike petroleum-based jet fuel, which releases carbon that would otherwise stay trapped underground, SAF recycles carbon already in circulation in plants, animals and the atmosphere. Washington’s per-gallon tax credit requires emissions at least 50% below those of conventional jet fuel.

Washington’s production capacity is below that of some larger facilities elsewhere. A Diamond Green Diesel plant in Texas can produce up to 235 million gallons of SAF annually, according to its partner Valero. That figure also represents capacity, not actual production.

With the minimum threshold being met, all Washington SAF producers will be eligible for the tax credit regardless of their volumes.

A startup called Twelve is already making the fuel in the central Washington city of Moses Lake. The company opened its AirPlant One facility last year and began commercially producing SAF this summer from captured carbon dioxide and water. The technology has the potential to create the most climate-friendly SAF available, potentially unlocking the largest state tax credits.

Nicholas Flanders, Twelve’s CEO and co-founder, welcomed the announcement.

“This is an extraordinary signal of support for our industry,” Flanders said via email. “Washington is building the leading foundation in the country for next-generation domestic fuel production, and Twelve is ready to build upon it.”

Twelve’s first-of-its-kind facility is designed to make up to 50,000 gallons of SAF per year. AirPlant Two, a much bigger plant that would make tens of millions of gallons a year, is in development. The company hasn’t said where it will be located.

Dutch-owned SkyNRG is building a SAF facility in Walla Walla, Wash., and plans to use renewable natural gas that’s captured at landfills and from dairy waste as a feedstock. Earlier this year, leaders said the company had secured key environmental approvals and plans to start commercial operations in 2030.

Washington’s relatively affordable hydroelectric power has historically helped attract climate tech companies. But growing electricity demand, including from data centers, is putting pressure on the region’s power supply.

Washington also faces competition from other states offering SAF tax incentives. Illinois and Minnesota already offer credits, and Nebraska’s program starts next year. Meanwhile, a federal credit was reduced from $1.75 per gallon to $1 after President Donald Trump returned to office.

Washington leaders tout other perks that could attract SAF production. It’s the only state that offers both a SAF tax credit and a clean fuel standard. Together, the policies help make cleaner jet fuel more cost-competitive by providing tax benefits and allowing SAF producers to earn credits they can sell to other fuel suppliers that need to meet the state’s emissions requirements.

The accelerator also supports efforts with Washington State University to develop regional feedstock supplies, including waste from logging and agriculture.

“Between our long history of aviation innovation, our intentional investments into the sector and our climate-forward policies, we’re making sure Washington is the best state in the country to produce sustainable aviation fuels,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5433. Amazon’s Ring tries again with a $250 flying home security drone and a $1,000 patrol robot

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 5:30 amNovember 10, 2026 at 5:49 am

Amazon’s Ring unveiled a $249.99 flying indoor security drone and a $999.99 mobile patrol robot for businesses, bringing back two ideas that stalled in earlier incarnations.

The Ring Drone Cam and Ring Rover Cam, announced Tuesday, are the first products under the Ring Robotics name, which the company calls “a new category of autonomous, mobile security.” Both devices use a system Ring calls AI Pilot to map a home or business, suggest spots worth checking, and find their own way around obstacles such as furniture and shelving.

The drone stays docked with its camera off until it’s sent out on a schedule, on demand, or automatically when another Ring device is triggered. The Rover patrols stores and offices, using a periscope camera to see over counters and shelving.

The Rover is available for preorder in the U.S. and is scheduled to ship Dec. 16. The Drone Cam is slated for Jan. 27, 2027, but Ring is only taking email sign-ups for now. The fine print notes that the drone hasn’t yet received the required authorization from the Federal Communications Commission.

Scheduled flights and patrols, and reviewing the Rover’s recorded video, require a Ring Protect subscription plan. Ring didn’t say which plans qualify.

Ring says customers wanted to see spots a fixed camera can’t reach, and rooms where they wouldn’t want one mounted.

“The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be,” said Jamie Siminoff, Ring’s founder and chief inventor, in a statement. “That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time.”

Ring unveiled a flying indoor camera called the Always Home Cam in 2020, also priced at $249.99. The company later opened an invitation list, but the device never went on general sale.

The original drone flew only along paths that owners mapped out with it in advance. Ring says the new one builds a floor plan as the owner carries it through the house, suggests spots to check, and plans its own routes.

The Rover Cam traces back to Astro for Business, a rolling security robot that Amazon launched in November 2023 at a starting price of $2,350. Amazon discontinued it less than a year later, refunding customers and shutting the robots off.

Astro for Business was a spinoff of Amazon’s Astro home robot, an Alexa-powered device on wheels that debuted in 2021 and can patrol the house on its own.

Ring says the new robot was inspired by Astro customers who said roving security was their favorite feature. The Ring team “leveraged the best of Astro” to build it, the company says. Ring is pitching the Rover as “not a home robot that also does security, but a purpose-built security robot.”

The original Astro for the home remains an invite-only product. Amazon has redeployed much of the Astro team to work on a new home robot, CNBC reported Sunday. In March, Amazon acquired Fauna Robotics, a New York humanoid robot startup, saying it would become part of a new Personal Robotics Group. Ring’s announcement doesn’t mention either effort.

The Rover also extends Ring’s push into commercial security, following a $5,000 surveillance trailer for parking lots that it unveiled in January. In security robots, it competes with companies such as Knightscope, which rents its robots through a subscription, and Cobalt AI. At $999.99, the Rover costs less than half what Astro for Business did.

On the security drone front, Indoor Robotics makes a ceiling-docking drone that patrols offices and warehouses, but flying security cameras for the home remain rare.

Siminoff, who launched Ring’s predecessor, Doorbot, in 2012 and sold Ring to Amazon in 2018, left the company in 2023 and returned last year to lead Ring and Amazon’s related home security businesses. Last month, Ring unveiled its first smart lock, a $249 deadbolt with no keyhole and a dial that recharges a dead battery by hand.

#5432. ‘Chinese companies are born to make money’: AI pioneer Kai-Fu Lee on the 3 biggest myths about China’s AI race efforts

Despite years of U.S. efforts to gain an edge over China in the AI race by restricting its access to the most advanced chips, one AI pioneer says America’s efforts have instead helped create a new generation of Chinese AI models that are quickly catching up to their American counterparts.

Kai-Fu Lee, an AI entrepreneur and former president of Google China, said in a Fortune Daily interview that U.S. export restrictions on the most powerful American chips have shaped Chinese companies’ strategy of building competitive AI models with fewer resources.

In response to these limits, which American companies don’t face, Chinese AI developers have built open-weight models that Lee estimates are now just six to 12 months behind those created by some of the biggest American AI companies, including OpenAI as well as Anthropic—which is reportedly preparing to go public as early as next week.

Yet when Americans think about China and the motivations of Chinese companies, they’re often getting some key things wrong, Lee said. In an interview with Fortune Daily published this week, he detailed three of the biggest misconceptions about China’s AI industry that he says have taken hold in America.

One of the biggest misconceptions about Chinese companies is that they are more focused on winning the AI race and becoming the first to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI)—widely considered the ultimate goal of AI development—than on building profitable businesses. That assumption is incorrect, Lee said.

“Chinese companies are born to make money. That’s the primary purpose,” Lee said. “It’s not so much to win AGI or win the race.”

He compared questions about the profitability of the current wave of Chinese AI developers like DeepSeek with those surrounding other Chinese tech companies like Pinduoduo, Meituan, and ByteDance. These tech giants’ business models were also initially questioned before they became some of China’s biggest companies.

“You may reasonably doubt China’s ability to do a breakthrough, which is valid. [The] U.S. is way ahead on that, but never doubt Chinese ability to find a way to make money,” he said.

A second misconception, Lee said, is that China’s embrace of open-weight models and open-source technology is part of an organized government effort to compete with America.

Instead, Lee said, market competition has driven the shift. He pointed especially to DeepSeek, a Chinese startup that stunned American AI companies in early 2025 by releasing a highly capable AI model by the same name that it claimed was trained using significantly less computing power than its American competitors.

“Chinese companies are venture funded just like the American companies,” Lee said. “They just want to serve their investors.”

Beijing has played a significant role in shaping the country’s AI industry. Investors with ties to the government participated in more than 140 Chinese AI deals in 2025, Fortune reported earlier this year, citing a Pitchbook analyst note.

China’s president, Xi Jinping, has also encouraged AI development in China. In 2025, Xi called for the country to develop “an independent, controllable, and collaborative artificial intelligence basic software and hardware system.”

Lee said in the interview that American companies have good reasons to spend more, including attracting the world’s best researchers and giving them enough computing power to experiment.

The third misconception, Lee argued, is that U.S. export controls are the main reason Chinese companies have shifted toward models that require less computing power, while American companies pour billions into data centers.

He argued that Chinese companies are naturally more frugal because they have different priorities than their American counterparts.

“The Chinese companies are naturally parsimonious; not just the startups,” he said, adding that “prudence and survival instinct” are more important to them than the pursuit of AGI.

That contrasts with the American approach, which emphasizes spending heavily on computing power to attract top researchers and accelerate AI development. Because of their resourcefulness, Chinese companies can develop and operate models for as little as one-tenth the cost of their American competitors, making their products attractive to businesses that don’t want to pay premium prices for AI services.

Despite the growing competitiveness of Chinese AI developers, American companies still produce more top-tier models and higher-impact patents, according to a Stanford University study. OpenAI and Anthropic are also the world’s most valuable AI companies.

OpenAI was valued at $1.25 trillion in a November funding round and is eyeing a potential IPO in 2027. Anthropic, meanwhile, is preparing to go public as early as next week in what could be one of the largest IPOs in history, seeking a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion.

Still, when DeepSeek showed it could compete with America’s leading AI developers, it helped boost the hopes of Chinese AI developers. Before DeepSeek, these developers believed their country was years behind the U.S. After DeepSeek showed off its model in 2025, sentiment shifted, he said.

“It’s a national pride thing, so people say, ‘Okay, we thought we were never going to catch up. Now we have a shot.’ So, it was quite a special moment,” he said.

Role: Reporter Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez is a reporter for Fortune covering general business news.

#5431. PitchBook to give early-stage startups free access, using their data to feed a new tool for VCs

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:23 amNovember 10, 2026 at 7:25 am

PitchBook announced a new program to give early-stage startups free use of its private-market data, if they share their financials and other company details.

The Seattle-based company says the new program, dubbed PitchBook for Startups, will feed PitchBook Origin, a new deal-sourcing product that helps venture capitalists and other investors find startups before they raise their first institutional round.

PitchBook announced both offerings Tuesday morning at Web Summit in Lisbon. Owned by Morningstar since 2016, the company has more than 3,000 employees and sells subscriptions to venture firms, private equity investors and dealmakers.

The launches come as first-time startup financings hit a record. There were an estimated 8,625 such deals in the U.S. through the third quarter, already more than the 8,507 in all of 2021, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. PitchBook attributes part of the surge to AI, which it says is making it easier to start companies.

The startup program is open to pre-seed and bootstrapped companies that haven’t taken money from a venture firm or other institutional investor, or raised a priced round, the type of funding round that sets a valuation.

Founders can use PitchBook to find investors who are active in their sector and stage, and to compare their valuation and growth against similar companies.

To keep their free access, startups must update their company information every quarter. PitchBook says that information can include financials, team growth and product milestones. Only “select portions” of that data will go into Origin, the company said, without saying which.

Origin covers about 25 million companies, including stealth, pre-funding and bootstrapped companies. About 15 million of them are new to PitchBook. It scores companies on how well they match an investor’s criteria and sends alerts when they show new activity.

“What’s been missing is visibility into the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see,” said Paul Santarelli, PitchBook’s chief solutions officer, in a statement announcing the products.

PitchBook didn’t disclose pricing for Origin, and the product’s web page currently asks investors to join a waitlist.

#5429. Allen Family Philanthropies gives $10M to hundreds of small arts groups across Washington state

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 9, 2026 at 2:56 pm

Allen Family Philanthropies and Seattle nonprofit ArtsFund awarded $10 million to 745 small arts and culture organizations across Washington state, and renewed the grant program for another $10 million next year.

The latest Community Accelerator Grant awards range from $2,500 to $25,000 and reach organizations in 37 of the state’s 39 counties. The 2027 renewal brings the program’s total to $50 million over five years.

For 2026, the program focused on groups with annual budgets under $1 million, which raised the average award by about 25%, from $10,753 last year to $13,423.

The change followed a sector analysis by Allen Family Philanthropies and SMU DataArts. It found that smaller arts groups lost an average of one staff position between 2023 and 2024, while organizations with budgets over $1 million added an average of five.

“The incredible reach of this program across our state, along with the significant findings from our report, show just how much this type of flexible support is needed to bolster Washington’s rich and diverse arts and culture sector,” said Lara Littlefield, executive director of Allen Family Philanthropies.

Of this year’s grantees, 496 are in Northwest Washington, 132 in Southwest, 67 in Eastern and 50 in Central Washington. Recipients include 12 of the state’s 29 federally recognized tribes, and more than 22% are in rural counties.

A handful of the organizations blend art and technology, including Tacoma’s Fablab Nonprofit ($25,000), Seattle-based Simulated Immersive Experimental Realities ($15,000) and Bellingham Makerspace ($2,500).

The Old Hotel Art Gallery in Othello, in Adams County, has received a $25,000 grant each year since 2024. The gallery used the money to pay staff a living wage, to keep operating until its annual fundraiser, and to renovate its historic building, which now brings in rental income.

Gallery director Samantha Copas said the 2025 award “truly kept our doors open.”

Allen Family Philanthropies, formerly known as the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation, was founded in 1988 by the late Microsoft co-founder and his sister, Jody Allen. Arts and culture is one of its core program areas, along with youth and the environment. Last year the foundation committed nearly $7 million to eight Seattle Center nonprofits, including KEXP and the Museum of Pop Culture, to expand youth access to the arts.

ArtsFund will hold a virtual webinar in the spring for organizations interested in applying for 2027 grants. Details will be posted here.

#5428. Before Megaspeed, there was Supermicro: The other Nvidia partner tied to China chip smuggling—and to Jensen Huang

Whether she was a spy, a fixer, or just a paramour of Jensen Huang, the name Alice Huang (no relation) has roiled the business world this week following reports that the two were having an affair. The revelation snowballed into Jensen’s shocking resignation Wednesday.

Now come reports that officials are looking into other companies Alice was working with. Bloomberg reported, based on an anonymous source, that the Department of Justice is running multiple probes into Nvidia. One is focused on antitrust issues and two others are focused on Megaspeed—where Alice Huang was a former top executive—and Super Micro Computer. Separately, the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Manhattan is probing whether entities linked to Alice Huang were involved in alleged efforts to smuggle Supermicro hardware laced with Nvidia’s red-hot GPUs into China. It is unclear whether that probe is tied to smuggling cases already brought in the U.S. or Asia. Neither Jensen Huang, Nvidia, nor Supermicro have been formally charged with any wrongdoing.

Supermicro stock tumbled 12% after U.S. markets opened this morning. The company did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Thus far, much of the speculation about Jensen Huang’s catastrophic downfall as the leader of Nvidia has centered on Megaspeed, the Singapore firm that reportedly became one of Nvidia’s largest buyers in Southeast Asia. But Supermicro, the San Jose server maker run by Charles Liang, Jensen Huang’s friend of three decades and an important partner to Nvidia, has been in under the microscope regarding export-control compliance and is being pulled along with Nvidia.

Fortune has reported on the Supermicro case since before federal agents arrested its co-founder in March, and that reporting shows a company with a documented track record of governance and compliance failures. Despite its history, Supermicro has remained in lockstep with Nvidia. Liang and Jensen have shared the stage together at Computex in Taiwan, where Jensen was photographed in 2024 with Alice at a cocktail bar.

In March, federal prosecutors charged Supermicro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and two others with allegedly routing about $2.5 billion in servers laced with Nvidia H200 and B200 GPUs to China through a Southeast Asian front company. Bloomberg later reported the front company is OBON, a Bangkok-based AI infrastructure firm, which has not been charged. Supermicro was not charged and has said it was a victim of the scheme.

Liaw, who immediately resigned his executive and board roles at Supermicro following his arrest, has pleaded not guilty. His trial was pushed to March 2027 after Liaw’s lawyers told the judge in his case that subpoenas issued to Supermicro could be material to Liaw’s defense. Nelson Boxer, Liaw’s attorney, declined to comment.

One of Liaw’s co-defendants in the smuggling case, Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, pleaded guilty in October, including to a charge that he deleted an encrypted messaging app from his phone on the day of the arrests. Sun’s attorneys did not respond to a request for comment, and it’s unclear if Sun has a cooperation agreement with the government.

There is no public evidence so far that the Supermicro and Megaspeed cases are directly connected but there are mounting threads. Thursday, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs issued a statement noting that the Singapore Police Force and Customs had initiated investigations into Megaspeed and Alice Huang and in doing so sought information from Supermicro. Supermicro only offered “limited cooperation,” Singaporean authorities said.

In a July 2025 meeting, Singapore officials raised this with U.S. authorities and asked for their assistance in getting Supermicro’s cooperation and have repeated the request “on several occasions” to the Department of Justice and the FBI.

“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement reads. In a statement to Fortune, a Supermicro spokesperson said it “has been responsive to inquiries and fully cooperated with U.S. and Taiwanese officials, while also voluntarily providing information and engaging with all requests from Singapore authorities to date.” The company added that “Megaspeed is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer.”

Supermicro’s export-control problems did not start with Liaw’s arrest, Fortune’s reporting has found. In 2006, the company pleaded guilty to illegally exporting computer equipment to Iran through a distributor in Dubai, mirroring the basic scheme prosecutors alleged in the Liaw case.

Liaw himself has been through the crisis wringer before. He left Supermicro in 2018 amid a board-led investigation tied to Supermicro’s Nasdaq delisting and an SEC probe of its accounting, which ended with a $17.5 million settlement in 2020. Liaw returned as a consultant in May 2021, became a full-time employee, and rejoined the board in December 2023.

In 2024, short seller Hindenburg Research accused Supermicro of accounting manipulation and export-control failures and the company denied the allegations. Ernst & Young then resigned as auditor mid-audit, saying it could no longer rely on management’s representations. A special committee recommended in December 2024 that Supermicro replace CFO David Weigand and the company agreed to do so “immediately.” The company didn’t name a successor until October.

As Fortune has reported, the Liaw indictment describes thousands of nonworking dummy servers staged in warehouses to fool auditors, contractors using hair dryers to peel off serial-number labels, and a compliance auditor who was off-site allegedly enjoying “entertainment” paid for by another company during an inspection. It also shows how the alleged scheme fed directly into Nvidia’s supply pipeline. In December 2024, Liaw allegedly told the front company that “the only way” to get Nvidia to commit B200 chip allocations was to create monthly forecasts. Nvidia is not accused of wrongdoing in the Liaw indictment.

After Liaw’s arrest, Supermicro’s board opened its own investigation, overseen by independent director Scott Angel and former audit committee chair Tally Liu (no relation to Liang’s wife and co-founder Sara Liu). In August, Supermicro said that probe found no evidence that current senior management knew about the alleged scheme to diver the chips. The investigation resulted in an unspecified number of terminations in sales, business development, and technical support, Supermicro said at the time, for failure to follow policies or the code of conduct.

Supermicro has also disclosed a grand jury subpoena covering the Liaw case and the company’s compliance program and internal controls, along with subpoenas or inquiries from the SEC, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and foreign authorities.

Through all that has beleaguered Supermicro, the company’s relationship with Nvidia has appeared to remain steadfast. This will all become a test for Supermicro’s new CFO, Mark Long, a former Western Digital finance chief who took over from Weigand last month and reports to Liang. The two tag-teamed the company’s most recent earnings call, when it reported record fiscal first-quarter revenue of $19.9 billion, well ahead of Wall Street consensus estimates. Supermicro also raised its full-year revenue forecast to $72 billion to $82 billion.

But now, Supermicro—and its CEO Liang—is losing an important champion in Nvidia’s Huang. Liang built much of Supermicro’s AI-era business through the close relationship with Nvidia combined with Supermicro’s almost supernatural ability to get the newest GPUs to market quickly. Liang has also maintained a public friendship with Huang that included joint keynotes in Taipei before adoring crowds.

Nvidia will now be led in the interim by Kress while an outside investigation into the foreign intelligence operation will be run by former acting SDNY U.S. Attorney Joon Kim and powerhouse law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.

Nvidia is slated to report third-quarter results on November 17, with Kress in place of Huang. House lawmakers have requested a closed-door grilling with Huang the following day. In January, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) is likely to lead the Senate Banking Committee, and she’ll have subpoena powers. Warren has already sought answers from Nvidia about Supermicro and chip smuggling in June and she re-upped her request this week.

Amanda Gerut is the west coast editor at Fortune, overseeing publicly traded businesses, executive compensation, Securities and Exchange Commission regulations, and investigations.

#5427. Data center developers brace for new reality as election backlash sinks in

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:25 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Data center developers already knew they had a public relations problem. This month’s midterm elections showed how much of a political problem it has become.

Voters approved data center restrictions in 44 of 45 local measures across a dozen states. Candidates who support stronger regulation of the facilities won 32 of the 34 gubernatorial races called so far. And political campaigns reportedly spent more than $380 million on TV ads referencing data centers, according to the Associated Press.

The results capped a year of accelerating resistance as tech giants plan to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on new facilities.

So what comes next? More outreach, more transparency and the expectation that states and local governments will pass data center rules, said leaders in the Pacific Northwest.

“We’ve been working and adapting our approach to meet the moment,” said John Wilson, chief financial officer of Sabey Data Centers, in an interview. “There used to be a time where we would say that our track record could speak for itself, and that’s clearly no longer the case.”

Communities nationwide have raised concerns about the facilities’ effect on rising electric bills, their water use for cooling electronics and the noise they generate.

Broader fears about artificial intelligence are also stoking the pushback, including worries that it will replace workers and appropriate human-created content, and that it can provide erroneous information, foster unhealthy relationships with users, or facilitate scams or terrorist attacks.

A renewed effort to regulate data centers is expected in January in Washington state — home to the headquarters of Sabey, Microsoft and Amazon.

Earlier this year, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, pushed legislation that included ratepayer protections, transparency on environmental impacts and clean energy requirements. Microsoft and the national Data Center Coalition opposed the bill, which failed.

“It’s going to be a very tech-heavy session,” Doglio said.

Before voters weighed in this month, tech companies launched efforts to assuage public fears.

In January, Microsoft released its “Community First AI Infrastructure” initiative, which includes promises to pay the company’s full power costs, reject local property tax breaks, replenish more water than it uses, train local workers and fund AI education and community programs.

Last month, Amazon announced its “Built Together” program, pledging to invest $1 billion over five years in the U.S. communities where it operates data centers, including support for education and civic projects. The initiative offers similar commitments to Microsoft’s on transparency and covering its energy costs.

Wilson said Sabey also works with communities to understand and meet their needs. When a proposed campus in Indianapolis triggered significant pushback, the company brought community members to Quincy, a central Washington data center hub, to tour a Sabey facility and hear from locals about their experience.

“It requires a lot of patience. It requires a lot of transparency in our communication,” Wilson said. Sabey’s Decatur Technology Park in Indianapolis is moving ahead, and the company aims to bring it online in 2030.

But the even bigger challenge now is statewide moratoriums and data center bans — a scale of resistance that is difficult to address even when there is local support.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. Umatilla, where Sabey is developing its first Oregon campus, declared a local state of emergency over the potential loss of investment and revenue, the Oregon Capital Chronicle reported.

Even with the surge in resistance, “we’ve been able to find our way through on every project that we’ve had,” Wilson said. “I’m knocking on wood as I say that.”

Corporate commitments alone may no longer be enough to win public confidence, said Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, in a GeekWire interview. Communities increasingly want laws requiring all data center developers to build responsibly — a shift he called a “watershed” moment, “but one we anticipated.”

“[P]eople want to see everyone who builds a data center do it in a responsible way,” Smith added, “and they feel that the only way that one can obtain that result is to have some new laws that are put in place.”

Come next year, that could include Washington and impact local tech giants, Sabey and others. Baxtel, a data center industry research firm, lists 29 Microsoft facilities operating in Washington and four under construction, with Sabey operating eight facilities.

Amazon plans to build its first large-scale data centers in Washington, with proposed campuses in Walla Walla County and the Tri-Cities. Amazon did not respond to repeated requests for comment on this story.

Doglio said the next version of her bill will be more stringent. “We have to have a strong bill,” she said, adding that the public and members of her party are calling for it. Microsoft did not publicly specify which provisions triggered its opposition to the previous bill.

Wilson hopes any legislation, in Washington or elsewhere, allows flexibility and recognizes that data centers vary widely in size, impact and application. Sabey provides data center space and infrastructure for customers ranging from major cloud companies to corporations and community organizations.

“Describing all data centers as one thing is just not accurate,” Wilson said, “and it doesn’t understand the realities of the industry itself.”

Smith expressed optimism that U.S. lawmakers can find a middle ground that meets the needs of communities and tech companies.

“There’s plenty of room to draft laws that enable people to go forward and build responsible data centers without chilling the economic contributions these data centers make, especially to local communities,” he said.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5426. Super Micro, run by Jensen Huang’s friend, says Megaspeed was ‘never’ its customer

Super Micro Computer says that Megaspeed, the Singapore company at the center of the spy scandal that brought down Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, has never been one of its customers.

The assertion by Super Micro, whose cofounder was arrested earlier this year on charges of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, comes as observers look for possible connections between two companies whose business dealings with Nvidia are under scrutiny.

“Megaspeed is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer,” a spokesperson told Fortune in a statement. The company also said it “has been responsive to inquiries and has fully cooperated with U.S. and Taiwanese officials, while also voluntarily providing information and engaging with all requests from Singapore authorities to date.”

Supermicro’s statement came after Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said Thursday that the Singapore Police Force and Customs had opened investigations into Megaspeed and Alice Huang, a former top executive there who had an affair with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, and who some authorities believe was acting as a spy for China.

Singapore authorities said they had asked Supermicro for information and had received only “limited cooperation.” The ministry said the Supermicro cooperation matter was first raised with U.S. authorities on July 7, 2025 and then repeatedly afterward with the Department of Justice and the FBI.

Alice Huang, who isn’t related to ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, drew intense scrutiny after reports that she and the Nvidia co-founder were having an affair, which came out before his resignation on Wednesday. The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Manhattan is reportedly looking into whether entities linked to her helped smuggle Supermicro hardware with Nvidia GPUs into China. Multiple probes have been initiated into export control breaches related to Alice and her businesses, including Megaspeed. Jensen, Nvidia, and Supermicro have not been charged with wrongdoing.

However, Jensen’s downfall has cast a dark cloud over Supermicro at an intensely complicated moment for the hardware and liquid cooling tech company. One of Supermicro’s three co-founders, Charles Liang, is a longtime friend of Jensen’s and the two both hail from Taiwan. They’ve shared the stage at multiple massive Computex tech events in Taiwan, including in 2024 when Jensen was photographed having drinks with Alice. Both cofounded their companies in 1993 and Supermicro’s close relationship with Nvidia has been a boon for customers hoping to be first in line for the latest generations of high-performing chips Nvidia churns out.

Another Supermicro cofounder, Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, was arrested and charged in March along with two others for allegedly working to route about $2.5 billion in servers with Nvidia’s H200 and B200 GPUs into China through a Southeast Asian front company. Liaw has pleaded not guilty, and his trial has been pushed to March 2027. A co-defendant, Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, pleaded guilty in October. Supermicro has said it was a victim of the scheme and conducted an internal investigation finding no evidence current members of senior management were aware of the alleged conspiracy. Supermicro’s stock fell nearly 4% this week.

In August, prosecutors in Keelung, Taiwan indicted nine people over 130 Supermicro servers with Nvidia B300 chips that were allegedly cleared for shipment using forged data-center inspection records. Some 74 of the servers made it to China and customs intercepted the rest. The defendants include two former Supermicro Taiwan employees and a former Nvidia Taiwan employee, who face breach of trust and document forgery charges. In Taiwan, unauthorized AI chip exports to China aren’t currently considered a criminal offense, which is why the charges relate to forgery and breach-of-trust charges. Neither Nvidia nor Supermicro was charged.

The company said in a statement that it “maintains a robust compliance program and continues to work closely with authorities and industry partners to combat diversion and help protect American innovation.” The company has disclosed a grand jury subpoena and inquiries from the SEC, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and foreign authorities.
